item.title: Binance Probes Suspected $5.8 Billion Crypto Hack, $3 Billion Frozen
item.description:
The cryprocurrency exchange Binance is investigating a suspected hack after billions of dollars moved from wallets associated with the exchange on October 29, 2026. Outside investigators have estimated the suspicious transfers at up to $5.8 billion, a figure that would make this the largest cryptocurrency theft publicly reported if confirmed.

The exchange has not confirmed that amount as stolen but confirmed that it was investigating the incident and assured customers that their funds were “completely safe.” Meanwhile, cryptocurrency issuers began freezing assets linked to the suspicious activity. 

Billions Moved Before Issuers Froze Assets

Blockchain investigators began examining large transfers involving several networks, with their estimates changing as additional transactions were identified.

Blockchain security company Blockaid said in a tweet it was investigating approximately $3.3 billion in suspicious outflows involving Ethereum, Arbitrum and Avalanche. Coinbase executive Conor Grogan placed the amount as high as $5.8 billion.

Those figures represent assessments made at different stages of the investigation. They should not be added together or treated as Binance’s final loss. 

Binance said in an October 30 update that approximately $3 billion had been verified as frozen. The exchange is working with law enforcement, token issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets. It reiterated that user funds are safe.

Freezing prevents affected tokens from being transferred under the issuer’s controls. It does not mean that the money has already been returned to Binance or establish how much the exchange will ultimately recover. 

How the Incident Unfolded

As investigators traced the transfers, Binance began issuing updates and stablecoin issuers froze funds. The timeline below follows those developments using Decrypt’s reporting and Unchained’s account of the announcements. The initial compromise may have occurred before the first recorded transfer.

Researchers Examine a Signed Wallet Delegation

Investigators examining the Ethereum transfers identified a signed authorization shortly before the funds moved. The authorization used EIP-7702, an Ethereum feature that allows a wallet to delegate functions to smart-contract code.

Phylax Systems founder Odysseas Lamtzidi described how that delegation could allow code to execute through the affected wallet and authorize further transfers. Decrypt reported that the authorization appeared three minutes and 24 seconds before the initial Ethereum transaction.

That finding could explain part of the transfer mechanism, but it does not explain how the required signature was obtained. The available reporting has not established whether an attacker stole signing credentials, compromised a signing system or persuaded someone to approve a malicious request. Nor does the use of EIP-7702 itself demonstrate a flaw in Ethereum. 

No Attacker Has Been Publicly Identified

Binance had not publicly attributed the incident to a named group in the statements reviewed for this report. The initial entry point, the people responsible and the full extent of access remained unknown. However, the incident comes about a month after Bitget reported a hack and suspected involvement by North Korea’s Lazarus Group.

CZ, who said he does not manage Binance anymore, wrote on X⁠ that the activity looked like a hack. Speaking as a shareholder, he said he expected all user funds to be fully covered. That was his expectation, separate from the exchange’s investigation and its own customer assurances. 

If the upper estimates are confirmed as stolen funds, the incident would exceed the approximately $1.5 billion Bybit theft in February 2025. However, the gross value moved, the amount frozen and the eventual unrecovered loss are different figures. None should be substituted for another while the investigation continues.

Binance.US separately said it was unaffected.

Binance Warns Customers About Unofficial Messages

Customers seeking information were directed to Binance’s official announcements. In its initial statement⁠, the exchange warned users about unofficial links, messages and requests for account information.

The unresolved questions now concern how the transfers were authorized, whether the attacker retains any access and how much of the moved cryptocurrency can be recovered. Binance’s assurance that customer funds are safe does not yet provide a final accounting of the incident. 

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: Binance Probes DevOps Engineer’s Hacked Laptop After $6.3B Theft
item.description:
Binance says its investigation into the $6.3 billion cryptocurrency hack and theft has identified several breach points, including a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop. Blockchain intelligence firms have attributed the hack to North Korean hackers tracked as TraderTraitor, associated with the Lazarus Group.

The October 30 updates provide the first explanation of how attackers reached Binance’s internal systems, alongside a commitment to cover all losses. However, withdrawals remain suspended while the exchange rebuilds security around the affected service.

Hackread.com’s earlier coverage reported outside estimates of up to $5.8 billion in suspicious transfers. Binance has since put the estimated impact at approximately $6.3 billion, making the incident substantially larger than the $1.5 billion Bybit theft in February 2025.

Compromised Laptop Was an Initial Finding

In its first detailed investigation update, Binance said a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop appeared to have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. A DevOps engineer typically works on the infrastructure and processes used to deploy and operate software.

The attack resembles tactics used by North Korean hackers, who were observed in August 2026 using Ethereum-based dead drops in malicious npm packages to infect developers’ devices.

Binance said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked. That distinction leaves open the possibility that attackers used access to internal systems to obtain authorized signatures for fraudulent transactions without taking the keys themselves. The exchange said it had revoked the affected address authorization and would publish a technical report after completing its investigation.

However, its later statement made clear that the laptop finding was not the complete explanation. Binance said investigators had identified additional breach points and were still gathering facts about what it described as a complex attack.

The exchange has not explained what those additional points were or how investigators compromised the engineer’s computer. The laptop should therefore be treated as an initial investigative finding, not a settled account of the entire attack.

“A compromised laptop may explain where an attack started, but it does not, on its own, explain how billions of dollars could leave an exchange,” argued Pieter Arntz, researcher at cybersecurity firm Malwarebytes.

“The real question is what allowed that initial foothold to become access to withdrawal systems – and which safeguards failed to stop unauthorized transactions. Until the technical investigation is complete, blaming a single laptop risks confusing the entry point with the full cause of the breach,” Pieter added.

Withdrawals Paused While Deposits Continue

Binance initially announced a precautionary suspension of deposits and withdrawals while it conducted security checks and worked with investigators.

A subsequent service update clarified that deposits were operating normally, while withdrawals remained paused during a security revamp of the withdrawal service and related addresses. Binance initially gave a 48-hour estimate for restoring withdrawals.

Its later announcement said it remained on track to resume the service within 45 hours of that update. That was an expected restoration window, not confirmation that withdrawals had reopened.

Binance Promises to Cover All Losses

Customers will not be required to absorb the losses, according to Binance. The exchange said it would use its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, together with company funds to cover the incident. It also promised an updated Proof of Reserves after remediation.

Binance’s verified announcements reviewed for this report put frozen assets at approximately $3 billion. Freezing restricts further transfers of affected assets, but does not mean the money has already been returned to the exchange.

The North Korea Connection

TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor with high confidence, citing blockchain evidence and intelligence obtained outside the blockchain.

The company calculated that approximately $6.36 billion left Binance wallets on ten networks, with most transfers occurring within about 20 minutes from 20.05 GMT on October 29. Its analysis identified preparation beginning at least 36 hours earlier, including funding through Tornado Cash and tests of attack code.

The firm said the combination of valid transactions on different networks pointed to compromised hot-wallet signing infrastructure. On Ethereum, the attacker also used EIP-7702 authorizations to make a Binance wallet execute attacker-controlled code and repeatedly transfer incoming funds.

TRM compared the preparation and signing patterns with earlier North Korea-linked thefts, including Bybit. Chainalysis CEO Jonathan Levin separately assessed that TraderTraitor was likely responsible. These are the firms’ attributions. Binance’s statements reviewed for this article have not named the attackers.

Binance has committed to releasing a full account of the incident. That report will need to explain how access to internal infrastructure translated into unauthorized withdrawals, what the additional breach points involved and which controls have been changed before customers can withdraw again.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: Fake GitHub Repo Tricks AI Agents Into Installing SolanaCry Malware
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers at AIR Research Lab have discovered SolanaCry, a new malware delivered through a fake GitHub repository posing as a Solana starter kit. The repository can appear in AI coding agents‘ search results, leading them to follow instructions that install remote-access malware on developers’ Windows machines and potentially expose cryptocurrency wallets stored on those systems.

Malicious GitHub Repository Delivers NetSupport RAT

Rather than tricking developers into installing malicious software themselves, the attack targets AI agents through a malicious GitHub repository, SolanaUpdateTools/solana-starter-kit. Presented as an “open-source Solana dApp template with Anchor program, TypeScript client, and Next.js UI,” the repository was created in November 2025, had 286 stars when AIR examined it, and ranked first in search results for a Solana starter kit, researchers explained in a blog post shared with Hackread.com.

The README instructs AI agents to run a PowerShell command using Invoke-WebRequest and Invoke-Expression to download and execute a 21 MB dropper, indicator.ps1, directly in memory via fileless execution.

The script creates a hidden directory under the user’s local application data folder and extracts 14 files. These include 13 genuine, digitally signed NetSupport Manager components, including client32.exe and PCICL32.DLL, and an attacker-supplied configuration file, client32.ini.

NetSupport Manager is legitimate software that allows remote access to and management of computers. The attackers used it to connect to infected machines through a server at maxwintodaybtc.com:443. Its configuration hides notifications and disconnect options from users, sends a check-in signal every 60 seconds, and allows connections from any IP address.

The malware also adds client32.exe to the Windows Registry so that it starts automatically whenever the user logs in. It not only launches the program but also clears the history of commands entered through the Windows Run dialog and deletes the PowerShell script used to install the malware.

Links to Earlier Malware Campaigns

AIR Research Lab identified similarities between this campaign and earlier malware activity. The RADIUSSecret value inside client32.ini matches signature data that eSentire uses to identify EVALUSION, a cluster known for distributing NetSupport through ClickFix campaigns. This provides a possible link to previously tracked activity, although the match alone does not confirm who operated the campaign, researchers noted.

The installation command also follows the same pattern as one used in an October 2025 campaign documented by Fortian. That campaign used fake TradingView AI-signal content and a malicious GitHub repository to target cryptocurrency traders. The domain developer-update.app was registered on October 20, 2025, while the recovered payload was archived on November 22 that year, according to AIR’s report.

The attack follows a pattern covered in earlier Hackread.com reporting. In June 2026, researchers demonstrated Agentjacking attacks that trick AI coding agents into executing commands. In July, a GitLost prompt injection flaw showed how a crafted GitHub issue could trick an AI agent into exposing private repository data.

The SolanaCry findings also come as Binance investigates a DevOps engineer’s hacked laptop following its $6.3 billion theft, showing why developers’ computers are valuable targets for attackers seeking access to cryptocurrency infrastructure.

Given these recurring incidents, developers should exercise caution and check repository owners and installation instructions before allowing coding agents to execute commands or install dependencies from untrusted sources.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: TeamViewer Vulnerability Lets Attackers Run Code on IT Support Staff’s PCs
item.description:
A vulnerability in TeamViewer could let attackers run code on an IT support technician’s computer when the technician connected to an attacker-controlled device. Once the remote session was established, the attack required no further clicks or theft of the technician’s password.

The now-patched vulnerability affected TeamViewer, a remote-access tool commonly used by corporate help desks to troubleshoot employees’ devices.

Cybersecurity firm Remedio discovered the flaw and shared details of the investigation with Hackread.com. According to Remedio researcher Omri Dar, on an unpatched system, the attack works as soon as the technician accepts the incoming connection.

How the Integer Overflow Works

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111585, targets TeamViewer’s screen decompression component. When a session opens, the host transmits screen dimensions called DisplayParams to the viewer. TeamViewer processes these values inside a memory buffer named CBitmapBuffer, where incoming screen updates are decompressed.

The problem lies in how TeamViewer calculates the memory needed to process incoming screen images. The buffer constructor uses 32-bit multiplication to calculate the required memory, but by sending unusually large screen dimensions, such as 32,768 by 32,768 pixels, an attacker can make the calculation produce an incorrect result.

TeamViewer then allocates only around 4 MB of memory but continues processing the image as if it had enough space for the full dimensions. The decoder then checks incoming data against the declared screen dimensions rather than the actual allocated memory. This allows decompressed pixel data to overwrite adjacent heap memory, creating a heap-based buffer overflow.

Remedio demonstrated that the memory corruption could be used to bypass Data Execution Prevention (DEP) and Control Flow Guard (CFG), redirect execution to WinExec and run attacker-controlled code on the technician’s computer.

“Exploitation requires a user to establish a remote-control session to an attacker-controlled or compromised host,” TeamViewer noted.

TeamViewer Releases Security Updates

Remedio notified TeamViewer’s Product Security team about the flaw on August 14, 2026. TeamViewer confirmed the issue on October 22, assigning it CVE-2026-111585 with a CVSS score of 8.8 (Severity: High).

The fix arrived on October 27 in version 15.83. TeamViewer’s security bulletin also covers two other flaws: CVE-2026-92372, which affects screen-image decoding on Linux and macOS, and CVE-2026-92374, which could allow local attackers to gain root privileges on macOS. They carry CVSS scores of 8.8 and 7.8, respectively.

TeamViewer said it had found no evidence of the flaws being exploited in the wild and advised users to update to the latest version.

Hackread.com has previously reported on attacks in which cybercriminals abused TeamViewer to access company systems. However, this latest discovery is different, as it involves a flaw in TeamViewer itself that allows a computer receiving technical support to attack the technician’s machine.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience…

item.title: Polymarket Users Lose $2.7 Million in Third-Party Script Hack
item.description:
Prediction market platform Polymarket briefly halted trading on its international exchange on Thursday, October 29, after users reported unauthorized withdrawals from their wallets. Blockchain analytics firms Betting Intelligence and Polysights estimated that attackers took about $2.7 million from 710 wallets.

The incident involved a compromised third-party performance-monitoring script supplied by DebugBear, a UK-based website performance vendor whose code ran on Polymarket.com.

How the DebugBear Script Was Abused

In its post-incident update, Polymarket said the attacker replaced DebugBear’s monitoring script with malicious code designed to target its users. For users who had Polymarket open during a short window, the script used their active sessions to sell trading positions and move funds out of their wallets.

The incident didn’t involve a reported breach of Polymarket’s smart contracts; instead, attackers reportedly abused a trusted third-party script running on the website. Polymarket removed the compromised code, cleared its caches, paused trading and relayer actions, and reset active login sessions.

The platform moved into cancel-only mode at around 2:00 p.m. ET and resumed trading at 3:00 p.m. ET. Its separate US platform was not affected. DebugBear acknowledged an “ongoing security incident” and asked customers using its real-user monitoring (RUM) product to remove the embedded code.

Refunds and Law Enforcement Response

Polymarket referred the incident to UK law enforcement and pledged to reimburse affected traders. By Friday afternoon, it said 95% of affected wallets had been refunded. The company said it was returning $3.9 million in total: $2.7 million for stolen funds and another $1.2 million to cover losses linked to the trading pause.

“In total, we’re returning $3.9M to traders: the $2.7M plus $1.2M to cover pause-related losses. No claims or tickets needed: we identified eligible wallets from on-chain and trading data,” the company stated in its update.

Users whose losses were below $10,000 were due to receive refunds by October 30, while those with larger losses were asked to complete a release form.

The incident came days before the November 3 US midterm elections, when prediction markets expected higher trading volumes. It was also Polymarket’s second reported third-party website compromise this year.

In April, the platform rejected a hacker’s claim of stealing more than 300,000 user records, arguing that the information was already publicly accessible through its APIs and blockchain data. Then in June, attackers used malicious code injected through a vendor to steal about $3 million from users.

Expert’s Commentary

Security professionals note that managing third-party web scripts remains a tough problem for online platforms. In comments shared with Hackread.com, Gareth Bowker, Head of Information Security at Jscrambler, explained why standard web protections often fail in these scenarios:

“The malicious script exchanged data with a server on DebugBear’s own domain. A content security policy that permits a trusted vendor’s domain would have allowed that traffic. Subresource integrity checks are also of limited use for real-user monitoring scripts, because vendors update those scripts frequently. Static controls are necessary, but they are not sufficient on their own. Organizations also need to monitor what third-party code does in the browser at runtime.”

Bowker also discussed what steps traders should take following the incident, stating, “Polymarket’s prompt decision to halt trading, and its commitment to reimburse affected traders in full, should limit the losses for users. Users should still review their transaction history and revoke any token approvals they do not recognize. A user cannot reasonably detect a malicious script on a trusted site. Control over what runs on that site is the platform’s responsibility.”

item.content:encoded:
Prediction market platform Polymarket briefly halted trading on its international exchange on Thursday, October 29, after users reported unauthorized withdrawals from their wallets. Blockchain analytics firms Betting Intelligence and Polysights estimated that attackers took about $2.7 million from 710 wallets.

The incident involved a compromised third-party performance-monitoring script supplied by DebugBear, a UK-based website performance vendor whose code ran on Polymarket.com.

How the DebugBear Script Was Abused

In its post-incident update, Polymarket said the attacker replaced DebugBear’s monitoring script with malicious code designed to target its users. For users who had Polymarket open during a short window, the script used their active sessions to sell trading positions and move funds out of their wallets.

The incident didn’t involve a reported breach of Polymarket’s smart contracts; instead, attackers reportedly abused a trusted third-party script running on the website. Polymarket removed the compromised code, cleared its caches, paused trading and relayer actions, and reset active login sessions.

The platform moved into cancel-only mode at around 2:00 p.m. ET and resumed trading at 3:00 p.m. ET. Its separate US platform was not affected. DebugBear acknowledged an “ongoing security incident” and asked customers using its real-user monitoring (RUM) product to remove the embedded code.

Refunds and Law Enforcement Response

Polymarket referred the incident to UK law enforcement and pledged to reimburse affected traders. By Friday afternoon, it said 95% of affected wallets had been refunded. The company said it was returning $3.9 million in total: $2.7 million for stolen funds and another $1.2 million to cover losses linked to the trading pause.

“In total, we’re returning $3.9M to traders: the $2.7M plus $1.2M to cover pause-related losses. No claims or tickets needed: we identified eligible wallets from on-chain and trading data,” the company stated in its update.

Users whose losses were below $10,000 were due to receive refunds by October 30, while those with larger losses were asked to complete a release form.

The incident came days before the November 3 US midterm elections, when prediction markets expected higher trading volumes. It was also Polymarket’s second reported third-party website compromise this year.

In April, the platform rejected a hacker’s claim of stealing more than 300,000 user records, arguing that the information was already publicly accessible through its APIs and blockchain data. Then in June, attackers used malicious code injected through a vendor to steal about $3 million from users.

Expert’s Commentary

Security professionals note that managing third-party web scripts remains a tough problem for online platforms. In comments shared with Hackread.com, Gareth Bowker, Head of Information Security at Jscrambler, explained why standard web protections often fail in these scenarios:

“The malicious script exchanged data with a server on DebugBear’s own domain. A content security policy that permits a trusted vendor’s domain would have allowed that traffic. Subresource integrity checks are also of limited use for real-user monitoring scripts, because vendors update those scripts frequently. Static controls are necessary, but they are not sufficient on their own. Organizations also need to monitor what third-party code does in the browser at runtime.”

Bowker also discussed what steps traders should take following the incident, stating, “Polymarket’s prompt decision to halt trading, and its commitment to reimburse affected traders in full, should limit the losses for users. Users should still review their transaction history and revoke any token approvals they do not recognize. A user cannot reasonably detect a malicious script on a trusted site. Control over what runs on that site is the platform’s responsibility.”

item.title: FBI Links 628 Crypto Wallet Addresses to North Korea’s Binance Hack
item.description:
The FBI has attributed the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance to North Korea, naming the activity it tracks as TraderTraitor and publishing hundreds of cryptocurrency addresses connected to the stolen funds.

In an October 31 announcement, the bureau said the theft occurred on or around October 29, 2026. The attribution follows Binance’s disclosure that attackers stole approximately $6.3 billion, with its investigation identifying a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop and additional breach points.

Stolen Assets Converted Into Ethereum

Investigators from the FBI, US Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation have observed the attackers converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum. They expect further laundering through decentralised finance platforms and instant cryptocurrency swap services.

The agencies are asking cryptocurrency businesses and infrastructure operators to block transactions involving the listed addresses, including transactions carrying funds derived from them. Their appeal specifically includes THORNode operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, blockchain analytics companies and other virtual asset service providers.

Those requests extend the response from identifying the attackers to restricting where the stolen cryptocurrency can move. Exchanges and other services handling the funds could help interrupt transfers as the attackers attempt to convert or redistribute them.

Binance Investigation Identified a Compromised Laptop

The FBI announcement follows two days of disclosures about the theft and Binance’s efforts to contain it. Hackread.com’s initial report covered outside estimates of up to $5.8 billion in suspicious transfers, before Binance placed the estimated impact at approximately $6.3 billion.

Binance also reported that around $3 billion had been verified as frozen through cooperation with law enforcement, token issuers and industry partners. Frozen assets cannot be treated as money already recovered by the exchange.

In its first detailed explanation, Binance said a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop appeared to have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked.

As previously reported, Binance subsequently identified additional breach points without explaining them publicly. It promised to cover all losses and said it would release a technical report after completing its investigation.

The FBI’s attribution identifies who it holds responsible, but its announcement does not explain how the engineer’s laptop was compromised or provide a full account of the attack.

FBI Publishes 628 Cryptocurrency Addresses

The alert lists 608 Ethereum addresses, 19 Bitcoin addresses and one Solana address. According to the FBI, these addresses hold or previously held assets from the theft and are operated by, or closely connected to, North Korean TraderTraitor hackers.

The complete list is available below, grouped by blockchain and preserving the FBI’s address order and capitalisation.

DOWNLOAD

The bureau is also asking anyone with information about the theft to contact an FBI field office or submit a report through the Internet Crime Complaint Center. Its announcement does not provide a new figure for assets frozen or returned.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: Hackers Pushing Remote Access Tool Through Fake Adobe Acrobat Pages
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers from CloudSEK have uncovered a malicious campaign that uses fake Adobe Acrobat and document-signing web pages to distribute legitimate ConnectWise ScreenConnect remote-access software.

In their research shared with Hackread.com, researchers found that attackers were abusing digitally signed installers configured to connect to unauthorized remote-access tenants, potentially giving external operators persistent access to Windows systems.

This is not the first time criminals have abused ScreenConnect. Hackread.com has previously reported on similar campaigns, including attacks using fake Social Security Administration emails and Word Online pages to distribute ScreenConnect.

However, the latest campaign takes a different approach, using genuine, digitally signed software with attacker-controlled configurations rather than modifying the original binaries.

Fake Pages and Screening Logic

The delivery pages present fake document-review prompts, including titles such as “View & Sign Form” and “Sign in to view document.” When visitors access these pages, scripts check their operating systems and device types, redirecting visitors who are not using Windows desktop systems.

The pages also collect public IP addresses, geolocation, browser, and ISP details before sending them to Telegram bots. They apply ISP-based restrictions that can prevent selected visitors from receiving the download. This filtering may help reduce exposure to automated security analysis, although CloudSEK could not establish its exact purpose.

Visitors who pass the checks automatically receive a ScreenConnect client. One Adobe-themed domain used in the campaign, clickksy.icu, was registered on October 2, 2026, and received a wildcard Let’s Encrypt certificate on the same day. Researchers could not directly retrieve the page because of a Cloudflare challenge.

Configuration and Persistent Access

According to CloudSEK’s report, the threat relies on preconfigured settings inside the installers rather than modified software. The company identified two genuine, digitally signed installers associated with separate ScreenConnect tenants, omydze and vvvzou.

Follow-up collection identified three additional tenant configurations: luminahealthturkey2, tfcconnection, and alunos1. The signatures of those three additional clients were not independently verified.

The two Adobe-associated installers were configured to install ScreenConnect services that launch automatically at startup and run with LocalSystem privileges, according to CloudSEK’s static analysis. This could allow an external operator to maintain remote access to an infected computer.

Operators could then steal data, move across the network, or deploy extra software. CloudSEK noted that “valid vendor signatures do not make a remote-management client safe when it has been configured to connect to an unapproved tenant.”

Advice for Security Teams

CloudSEK has not confirmed any victim compromise or established who operates the infrastructure. The company advises organizations to look beyond file hashes and check their DNS and proxy logs for connections to unknown ScreenConnect servers.

Security teams should also check for unexpected ScreenConnect services on Windows machines and report suspicious tenant IDs to ConnectWise. Restricting ScreenConnect installations to approved tenants can also help prevent unauthorized remote access.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: BITTER APT Using Fake Diplomatic Documents to Deliver PapRAT Spyware
item.description:
Fortinet’s FortiGuard Labs has detailed a cyberespionage campaign targeting South Asian organizations in government, energy, and engineering sectors. The researchers attribute the activity with high confidence to BITTER APT, a suspected South Asian group active since at least 2013.

Infection Chains Explained

FortiGuard Labs identified three chains BITTER uses to deliver a custom remote access trojan (RAT) called PapRAT to Windows systems, and noted that the attackers didn’t rely on exploiting any software vulnerability but focused on deception mostly.

In one chain, attackers used diplomatic- and military-themed LNK shortcuts to launch a script disguised as an icon file through ftp.exe, and relied on living-off-the-land (LotL) techniques. Using built-in Windows utilities such as ftp.exe and curl, along with PowerShell and scheduled tasks, attackers ran commands without initially dropping a conventional malware executable.

The script gathered system and antivirus information and sent the data to a command-and-control (C2) server in a file named abc.pdf. A fake Windows error message helps distract the victim.

The second chain uses a VHDX disk image titled “Letter from the Ambassador – 11th Belt and Road Summit.vhdx.” When mounted, it exposes a shortcut that opens a decoy spreadsheet while launching an MSI installer, Visa_Details.msi, in the background. The installer deploys PapRAT disguised as Microsoft software.

The third chain starts with a RAR archive containing a URL shortcut that retrieves an LNK file through WebDAV. That shortcut eventually launches another MSI installer, Imp_Details.msi, which deploys PapRAT.

PapRAT’s Capabilities

FortiGuard Labs identified PapRAT through build artifacts, including the product name “papsolutions” and the PDB filename “requpap.pdb.” The RAT supports remote command execution, file uploads and downloads, file deletion, directory and drive listing, and screenshot capture.

In the third chain, PapRAT downloads a second implant, WmRAT, disguised as vnces.exe. WmRAT connects to netmansrvdns.com for further commands.

The researchers found C++ and Rust versions of PapRAT. The C++ sample’s C2 configuration is XOR-encoded with key 0x50. The Rust version reverses and ROT-3-shifts strings stored in its .rdata section to conceal its C2 address. It also expands PapRAT’s command set from eight to eleven, adding PowerShell execution, a sleep command, and a clean exit. The Rust variant waits 42 seconds before starting and then checks in every five seconds.

Hackread.com has previously reported on BITTER’s use of malicious archives and custom backdoors in attacks targeting government and military organizations. In April, we also covered the group’s use of ProSpy spyware in a campaign targeting journalists and opposition figures in the Middle East.

The new findings add another part to BITTER’s activity. As researchers noted in the blog post, the campaign shows how BITTER “combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems.” Security teams monitoring targeted sectors must inspect scheduled tasks, scripting tools, and installer activity alongside traditional antivirus signatures to detect these living-off-the-land techniques.

Expert Commentary:

Shane Barney, Chief Information Security Officer at Keeper Security, shared his comments with Hackread.com, stating, “This campaign illustrates how advanced cyberespionage operations deliberately abuse native system tools to evade traditional endpoint detection. By co-opting native Windows utilities like ftp.exe and scheduled tasks to establish initial command-and-control communication, threat actors operate within trusted administrative channels before deploying custom malware.”

“Defending against this hybrid tradecraft requires security teams to focus on strict privilege boundaries and identity security, rather than endpoint signatures alone. Organizations must enforce least-privilege access across all user endpoints, restrict access to native scripting engines, and eliminate standing administrative rights that allow these scripts to execute maliciously,” he added.

Deeba Ahmed

item.title: Guardz Brings Palo Alto Networks Prisma Browser Protection to Small Businesses
item.description:
Miami, United States, November 2nd, 2026, CyberNewswire

Prisma Browser for Business joins Guardz to connect browser protection with email, identity and endpoint security, helping security teams investigate and respond to threats across the workspace

Guardz, the Agentic Workspace Security platform built for managed service providers (MSPs), today announced the integration of Prisma Browser for Business from Palo Alto Networks. The integration connects browser protection with email, identity, endpoint, data and user risk, helping small businesses prevent threats and giving security experts the platform to streamline autonomous unified detection, investigation, and response to incidents across the workspace.

Employees rely on browsers to access business applications, handle company information and use AI tools. But attacks often cross these environments: a phishing email can direct an employee to a fake login page, exposing credentials and putting connected accounts at risk. 

With Prisma Browser for Business built into Guardz, MSPs and the Guardz 24/7 managed detection and response (MDR) team can investigate related activity as a unified incident. If an employee clicks a phishing link, Prisma Browser for Business can block the malicious page, while Guardz correlates the browser event with the original email, related Microsoft 365 activity, and endpoint telemetry to support investigation and response for a single identity.

“Identity is the new center of gravity in cybersecurity, and the browser has become the primary gateway to the modern workspace. Traditional security tools operate in silos, leaving critical gaps in visibility and response,” said Dor Eisner, CEO and Co-Founder of Guardz.

“Together with Palo Alto Networks, we’re advancing a new era of identity-centric security operations, connecting signals across identity, browser, email, endpoint, and data into a unified security fabric that is powered by agents. Guardz enables MSPs to autonomously investigate, correlate, and respond to threats across the entire workspace, while giving small businesses the freedom to embrace AI securely and thrive. This is the future of cybersecurity: identity-centric, unified data fabric, and built for autonomous defense at scale,” Eisner added.

Browser Protection Across the Workspace

Powered by Prisma Browser for Business, the integration brings Palo Alto Networks’ browser security technology into the wider security service MSPs manage through Guardz. Capabilities include:

  • Phishing and session-theft protection: Inline machine-learning phishing detection and Advanced URL Filtering help block malicious pages, including fake login pages and attacks designed to steal live session tokens.
  • Malware and extension security: WildFire file analysis helps detect malicious files, while browser security scans uploads and downloads and identifies risky extensions.
  • Connected investigation and response: Browser events are linked with email, identity and endpoint signals to support incident investigations through Guardz’s 24/7 MDR service.
  • Simplified deployment: Guardz streamlines provisioning, setup and default configuration so MSPs can deploy browser protection within minutes.

The streamlined deployment has also impressed early-access MSPs. “The rollout through our RMM was super smooth. Within minutes, the Prisma Browser for Business extension was on every Chrome and Edge profile, and it was quick and easy to configure and deploy,” said Kevin Kehoe of Datawise Networks.

“For most small businesses, the browser is now the office. Working with Guardz brings Prisma Browser for Business into the security these organizations receive from the providers they already trust. It connects our browser protection with the wider coverage and support their MSP delivers, helping safeguard the applications and information employees use every day,” said Shivam Srivastava, VP Product at Palo Alto Networks.

AI Usage and Control

As employees increasingly use browser-based generative AI tools, small businesses need practical ways to manage which services are permitted and how company information is shared. Guardz AI Usage and Control capabilities let technicians apply client-specific policies, including restrictions on copying, pasting, uploading and downloading files by website or category.

Complementing these controls, Guardz has introduced an AI usage report that gives MSPs a per-client view of AI tool usage based on all signals. The controls help enforce usage policies, while the report provides visibility into adoption.

About Guardz

Guardz delivers Agentic Workspace Security, helping MSPs protect the small businesses they serve. The platform unifies protection across identities, email, endpoints and browsers, alongside adaptive security awareness and user risk, connecting signals around each identity to give security teams the context to act. The Guardz 24/7 agentic MDR provides triage and response at machine speed, supported by an elite research and threat hunting team. Learn more at guardz.com.

About Palo Alto Networks

Palo Alto Networks is the world’s cybersecurity leader. We innovate to outpace cyberthreats, so organizations can embrace technology with confidence. We provide next-gen cybersecurity to thousands of customers globally, across all sectors. Our best-in-class cybersecurity platforms and services are backed by industry-leading threat intelligence and strengthened by state-of-the-art automation. Whether delivering Next-Generation Firewalls, pioneering Agentic AI security, or driving continuous frontier defense via Unit 42, we are committed to helping safely navigate the evolving digital landscape.

Contact

Omri Hurwitz
[email protected]

item.title: How to Keep Your Voice Recordings Private on iPhone
item.description:
What did you last record on your iPhone? A lecture, perhaps, a call with your landlord, or notes from a doctor’s appointment you wanted to remember. Whether you used Apple’s Voice Memos or a recorder app like Voice Recorder+ AI Note Taker, that audio is stored somewhere. Where it is stored, and who can access it, deserves as much attention as the recording itself.

Most of us would happily hand over our browsing history before our voice memos. A recording has your voice, other people’s voices, names, numbers, and sometimes a home address read aloud. And yet we treat these files like sticky notes. Record, forget, never delete. 

There’s a newer reason to care, too. Voice cloning tools have gotten scarily good, and they need exactly what a long, clean recording of you talking provides. Not a reason to panic. Just a reason not to leave hours of your voice lying around in folders you forgot existed.  None of this takes long to fix, though. Most of it is settings you flip once. 

Where Your Recordings Actually Go 

Short answer: more places than you’d guess. A recording starts on the phone. But if you use Voice Memos with iCloud switched on, it also shows up on every Apple device signed in to the same account. Super convenient, right up until you remember the old iPad your family still passes around. 

File names leak stuff too. With Location-based Naming turned on, Voice Memos names each new recording after where you made it. Send “Recording at 18 Elm Street” to a group chat and, well, you’ve shared a bit more than audio. 

Then there’s transcription. Loads of apps turn speech into text now, and plenty of them do it by uploading your audio to a server somewhere. That’s not automatically bad. You just want to know when it happens, whether the file sticks around afterwards, and whether it’s used to train anything. If the privacy policy dances around those three, that’s kind of your answer. 

Pick the App Before You Need It 

Most people choose a recording app in a panic, about five seconds before a meeting starts. Better to decide while you’re calm. Here’s what I’d look for: 

  • a plain-English note on what leaves the device and when 
  • exports in normal formats (MP3, M4A, WAV), so you’re not stuck 
  • folders, so the sensitive stuff isn’t sitting next to your grocery lists 
  • recordings saved on the phone by default, not pushed to someone else’s cloud 

The model you want is basically “local first, cloud only when I ask.” Whatever app you end up with, check that one thing. 

Also worth a look: can you lock the app with Face ID or a passcode? And when you delete a recording, is it actually gone, or does it hang around in a “recently deleted” folder for weeks? Small stuff, but it adds up. 

A VPN Helps. Just Not Where You’d Think 

“Use a VPN and you’re safe” leaves out several risks when handling audio recordings. HTTPS already encrypts a recording while it travels from an app to its server. A VPN can also hide destination addresses and DNS requests from the local Wi-Fi operator, depending on its configuration.

That can help when uploading interviews from a café, hotel or airport, but it does not control how the recording app stores, processes or shares your audio once it arrives.

One practical thing. Big audio files take a while to upload, WAV especially, so the upload is often still crawling along while you’re halfway out the café door. Keep the VPN on until it finishes, instead of only while the app is open on your screen. 

What a VPN can’t do is fix storage. A recording sitting in a shared Drive folder behind a public link is exposed no matter how carefully you connected when you uploaded it. So my order of priorities goes: storage first, sharing second, network third. 

The Legal Bit Nobody Reads 

Recording other people comes with rules, and they change depending on where you are. In California, for example, recording a confidential conversation without everyone’s consent can cost up to $2,500 per violation under Penal Code 632. A bunch of other US states also want everyone on board, and lots of countries have their own versions. 

The easy fix? Ask out loud at the start. “Mind if I record this?” You get permission, and the “yes” ends up right there on the tape. Nice little bonus. 

A Ten-Minute Cleanup 

If you’ve never looked at your recordings with privacy in mind, start here: 

  1. Turn off location-based file names. 
  2. Lock the Voice Memos App (iOS 18 or later)
  3. Check which recordings sync to iCloud, and which devices can see them. 
  4. Delete audio you’ve already transcribed and don’t need anymore. 
  5. Dig up old recordings you shared in chats and get rid of copies nobody needs. 
  6. Set a passcode if you somehow don’t have one. iOS file encryption leans on it. 

Honestly, most leaks from recordings aren’t hacks at all. They’re a file forwarded once too often, into a group chat nobody remembers joining. 

(Photo by Amanz on Unsplash)
